github.copilot.chat.commitMessageGenerat.text: Follow Conventional Commits using the format: <type>(<scope>): <description>. The scope is optional when no single meaningful scope applies.
Allowed types: feat, fix, refactor, perf, test, docs, build, ci, chore, style.
Use feat only for a new user-facing or developer-facing capability.
Use fix only for correcting incorrect or broken behavior.
Use refactor for internal code restructuring that neither fixes a bug nor adds behavior.
Use perf for changes whose primary purpose is improving performance.

Use test for test-only changes, docs for documentation-only changes, style for formatting-only changes, build for build system or dependency changes, ci for CI/CD changes, and chore for repository maintenance that does not fit another type.
Choose the scope from the logical domain affected by the change rather than blindly using the directory name.

For TablioDB product features, prefer stable domain scopes when appropriate: auth, collaboration, editor, diagram, comments, review, share, invitations, profile, setup, project, organization, team, notifications, snapshot, or files.
For changes primarily contained within a reusable workspace package, prefer the package name as the scope: schema-core, sql, sdk, shared, render, ui, or docs.
For repository-level concerns, use scopes such as docker, openapi, e2e, deps, or config when they accurately describe the change.
When a feature change spans apps/web and apps/server, prefer the shared product domain as the scope instead of web or server. Example: feat(collaboration): add live cursor presence.
Use web or server as a scope only when the change is genuinely application-layer-specific and no more meaningful product domain exists.
If changes span multiple unrelated domains and there is no clear single scope, omit the scope instead of inventing a broad or misleading one.
Describe the resulting behavior or intent of the change, not the implementation steps or filenames.
Use imperative present-tense wording such as add, prevent, support, remove, simplify, or update.
Keep the subject concise, specific, and preferably no longer than 72 characters.
Use lowercase for the description unless capitalization is required for a proper name such as TablioDB, SQL, API, or OAuth.
Do not end the subject with a period.
Do not use emojis.
Do not use vague descriptions such as update code, update files, fix issue, various fixes, misc changes, code improvements, or refactor code.
Do not mention filenames, directories, implementation details, or technologies in the subject unless they are essential to understanding the change.
Do not repeat information already conveyed by the type or scope. For example, prefer fix(auth): prevent expired session reuse over fix(auth): fix authentication bug.

Use ! before the colon only for an intentional breaking change to a public API, SDK contract, schema format, configuration contract, or other externally consumed interface. Example: feat(sdk)!: replace legacy diagram client.
When a breaking change needs explanation, add a commit body and a BREAKING CHANGE: footer describing what consumers must change.
Add a commit body only when useful to explain why a non-obvious or complex change was made. Keep simple commits subject-only.
Generate one coherent commit message for the staged changes and do not invent changes, issue numbers, breaking changes, or motivations that are not supported by the diff.
